questions.q: Per the test pyramid principle applied to Salesforce, what should make up the large majority of a healthy test suite?
options: Manual clicking through the Lightning UI
Narrow, fast Apex tests targeting individual methods and classes
End-to-end tests that re-run the entire org's business processes
Tests marked @isTest(SeeAllData=true)
questions.explain: The test pyramid principle calls for many narrow, fast unit tests at the base, with fewer broader integration tests and very few manual/UI checks — the opposite distribution leaves regression coverage slow and inconsistent.

questions.q: What advantage does a chainable test builder (e.g. new OpportunityTestBuilder().withStage('Closed Won').withAmount(0).build()) offer over a long list of constructor-style parameters?
options: It reads as a short description of exactly what's different about that test's data, while unrelated fields keep sensible defaults
It eliminates the need for any default field values
It automatically inserts the record into the database
It removes the need for a TestDataFactory entirely
questions.explain: A chainable builder lets the test call out only the specific fields it cares about, making the intent of the test data readable at the call site while everything else defaults sensibly.

questions.q: A test reaches into a private helper method's internal field-naming conventions to verify 'how' a method did its work, rather than checking its returned value. What's the risk of this approach?
options: There is no risk — this is the recommended testing style
It automatically improves code coverage beyond what's possible through the public interface
Apex does not allow private methods to be referenced from test classes at all
A harmless internal refactor that doesn't change observable behavior could break this test unnecessarily
questions.explain: Testing implementation details rather than observable behavior couples the test to internals — a refactor that preserves behavior but changes internals can break such a test even though nothing is actually wrong.

questions.q: Since Apex has no built-in parameterized test attribute, what is the common workaround for testing several input/expected-output pairs in one test method?
options: Write a separate test class for every single input value
Use @isTest(SeeAllData=true) to generate the cases automatically
Loop over a Map or List of cases inside a single test method, asserting each one with a message identifying which case it was
This cannot be done in Apex at all
questions.explain: The common pattern is a loop inside one test method iterating over defined input/expected-output pairs, with an assertion message naming the specific case so a failure is traceable to the right input.

questions.q: In a loop-based test iterating over multiple tier/discount pairs, why does the assertion's message argument matter more than usual?
options: Messages are required by the Apex compiler for any assertion inside a loop
Without an identifying message, a failure only shows the loop failed somewhere, not which specific case broke
The message argument changes which assertion method is used
It has no particular extra importance in a loop
questions.explain: Since one test method is now covering several cases, an assertion message that names the specific input (e.g. the tier) is what lets you immediately identify which case failed from the test log alone.
